title: Hi, what's your name?
goal: Greet people at the right time of day, say your name, ask how someone is, and see why the word "I" can almost always be dropped.
bekal: greet with *cześć*, *dzień dobry*, and *dobry wieczór*, each in its proper place
give your name with *nazywam się* and ask other people theirs
use *być* (to be) for every person, and know when to drop the pronoun

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Pierwszy dzień w szkole językowej
dialogs.intro: The first day of a course at a language school in Kraków. Two new students sit down next to each other.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Cześć! Nazywam się Budi. A ty?
lines.id: Hi! My name's Budi. And you?
lines.literal: hi! I-name self Budi. and you?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: I'm Ania. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Tak, jestem z Krakowa. A ty? Jesteś Chińczykiem?
lines.id: Yes, I'm from Kraków. And you? Are you Chinese?
lines.literal: yes, I-am from Kraków. and you? you-are Chinese-man?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nie, jestem Indonezyjczykiem. Jestem z Dżakarty.
lines.id: No, I'm Indonesian. I'm from Jakarta.
lines.literal: no, I-am Indonesian-man. I-am from Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dziękuję bardzo! Do zobaczenia jutro, Aniu.
lines.id: Thanks a lot! See you tomorrow, Ania.
lines.literal: I-thank very! until seeing tomorrow, Ania!

notes: **Cześć works both ways.** One word for "hi" and "bye" — like Italian *ciao*. But it is **informal**: for friends, people your age, and young people. To strangers or older people, the greeting is *dzień dobry*.

**Jak się nazywasz is not "what is your name".** Literally it's "how do you call yourself". *Nazywać się* is a full verb that always comes with *się* — a little word meaning "oneself". That's why the answer is a verb too: *nazywam się Budi*.

**There's a shorter way.** *Jestem Ania* — "I'm Ania" — is just as correct and actually more common among friends. Save *nazywam się* for slightly formal introductions: in class, at work, on the phone.
**Miło mi** literally means "pleasant to me", and it's a complete sentence — no "I" and no "is" in it. The reply is *mnie również* ("to me too") or simply *miło mi*.
**Watch out for the biggest trap:** *tak* means **yes**. "No" is *nie*. Both words are short and easy to swap in a hurry, and swapping them is no small mistake.

**The pronoun is missing.** Notice: *nazywam się*, *jestem*, *dziękuję* — none of them has *ja* (I) in front. The verb ending already shows who is speaking, so the pronoun isn't needed. *Ja jestem Budi* isn't wrong, but it sounds like stressing "**I'm** Budi".

**Jesteś Polką? Jestem Indonezyjczykiem?** A nationality after *jestem* takes a special ending (*-ą* for women, *-em* for men). That form is called *narzędnik*, and you'll deal with it properly in Unit 2. For now, just accept the form as it is.
**Nationalities are capitalized.** *Polka*, *Indonezyjczyk*, *Chińczyk* — just as in English. Language names, though, are lowercase: *polski*, *indonezyjski*.

**Aniu**, not *Ania*. When calling someone by name, Polish uses a special form called *wołacz*. For women's names ending in *-a*, the ending changes to *-u*: *Ania → Aniu*, *Marta → Marto*. Just recognize it for now; it won't be tested.

grammars.title: Być — the verb "to be"
body: The first verb you must master, and the only one whose forms really have to be memorized whole.
after: Look at the ending pattern: **-m** for I, **-sz/-ś** for you, **-my** for we, **-cie** for you plural. The same pattern shows up in every other verb in this course, so spotting it now saves a lot of memorizing later.
⚠️ *są* is read **son** — the letter *ą* is a nasal *o*, not an *a*. One of the most persistent mistakes, because the letter's shape fools the eye.
There are two words for "they": ***oni*** if the group has **at least one man**, ***one*** if it's only women, children, or things. This distinction comes back again and again in Polish.

grammars.title: Personal pronouns — and why they're often dropped
body: Polish has a full set of personal pronouns, but in ordinary sentences they're mostly **left out**.

head: Pronoun
Say it
Meaning
When is it used?
rows: often — the verb form is the same

after: Why are *on*, *ona*, *oni* used so often? Because the verb form for all three is **exactly the same** (*jest*, *są*), so without the pronoun you can't tell who is meant.
*Jestem*, on the other hand, can only mean "I". Adding *ja* isn't wrong, but it sounds like raising your voice: *Ja jestem Budi* = "**I'm** Budi (not him)".

blocks.text: These twelve phrases cover almost everything you need on day one. Memorize the sound, not the structure — the grammar will follow in later units.

Please. / Here you are. / You're welcome.
yak to sheh MOO-vi po POL-skoo
How do you say that in Polish?

blocks.title: One word, three uses
items: *Proszę* is the most versatile word in Polish. It means **"please"** when asking (*Kawę, proszę* — coffee, please), **"here you are"** when giving (offering a chair with a *proszę*), and **"you're welcome"** in reply to thanks.
There's a fourth use: *Proszę?* with rising intonation means "sorry, what was that?" — a polite "pardon?".

sections.title: Polite or informal: Pan, Pani, and ty

blocks.text: Polish draws a sharp line between talking **informally** and talking **politely** — English has no such line at all. Choosing wrong won't make you incomprehensible, but it feels like calling your professor "dude".

head: To whom
Form of address
Example
rows: A man you don't know well
A woman you don't know well

blocks.text: Look at the verb form: with *pan* and *pani* you use the **he/she** form (*ma*), not the **you** form (*masz*). Polish is polite by speaking *about* the person rather than *to* them — like saying "Would sir like…?" in English.

blocks.title: A practical rule for beginners
items: Greet anyone you don't know with *dzień dobry*, not *cześć*. This is almost never wrong.
Wait for the Polish person to offer *ty* first (*Możemy na ty?* — "can we use *ty*?"). Accepting is polite; jumping ahead may not be.
Among students, in language class, and among people your age, *ty* is used right away with no ceremony.
